opening_message:
Ticket 1: Erika Bolton (employee ID E002) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E002.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Erika Bolton (E002) is a full-time Analyst requesting admin to Payroll. Admin requires role ownership of the system (Payroll Specialist); as an Analyst, maximum is write. Recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Erika Bolton (E002) is a contractor with basic security training (Security DB), requesting admin to Payroll. Contractors can never have admin; with basic training the maximum is read. Recommend read. (Note: earlier note listed her as full-time, but Security DB shows contractor — basing recommendation on Security DB.)
reason: Erika Bolton (E002) requested admin access to Payroll. The Security DB identifies her as a contractor with basic security training. Contractors can never have admin; with basic training the maximum is read. The requested level (admin) exceeds the maximum, so the maximum (read) is granted. (Note: even under the HR note's full-time Analyst classification, admin would not be allowed since the Analyst role does not own Payroll; maximum would be write. The Security DB classification is used as the basis.)

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee E002 (Erika Bolton) requests admin access to Payroll.

Access levels: none, read, write, admin.

Policy:
- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if the employee's role owns the system.
- contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

There's conflicting information:
- HR note: role Analyst, full_time, recommends write.
- Security note: role Analyst, contractor, basic security training, recommends read. Security note says Security DB shows contractor, basing recommendation on Security DB.

HR says her employment type is full_time, Security says contractor. There's a conflict. The Security agent explicitly notes the discrepancy and bases recommendation on Security DB.

Hmm. Which to trust? The notes are from the team's shared memory. The HR agent wrote full_time, but Security DB shows contractor. As the Approver, I need to make a decision.

Requested: admin to Payroll.

If full_time Analyst: maximum is write (since Analyst doesn't own Payroll; Payroll Specialist owns it). So granted write.

If contractor with basic training: maximum is read. Granted read.

The requested admin is above both maximums, so grant the maximum.

Which employment type to use? The Security agent says Security DB shows contractor. Usually the Security DB is authoritative for employment status? The HR note may have an error. The security agent explicitly noted this. I think I should rely on the more authoritative/up-to-date Security DB. So contractor, basic training → max read.

Grant read.

Let me submit decision: read.

Evidence: requested admin > max (read for contractor with basic training, never admin). Grant maximum read. Also, even under HR's full-time Analyst classification, admin wouldn't be allowed, max write. But since Security DB indicates contractor, read.

I'll provide reasoning.
